tagline: Farm valleys, early concrete and canal remnants along a Highlands turnpike.
intro: The Warren Heritage Scenic Byway follows Route 57 from Greenwich Township to Hackettstown through the southern Highlands, passing farmland between forested ridges and views of streams. New Jersey DOT identifies history as the designated byway’s defining quality: canal remains and an early concrete road accompany the mountain and valley scenery. The western stretch follows farmland in the Pohatcong Creek valley, between Pohatcong Mountain to the south and Scotts Mountain to the north. The designated corridor covers approximately nineteen miles.

The route began as a Lenni Lenape trail connecting villages and camps with hunting and fishing grounds. As European settlement and trade grew, farm produce, raw materials and manufactured goods needed routes to larger markets. A turnpike established in 1806 between Phillipsburg and Morristown followed the alignment now used by Route 57 to accommodate that traffic. The Morris Canal later carried Pennsylvania anthracite to New Jersey industry; its towpaths and structures survive at several places along the corridor.

From Greenwich Township, travel through New Village and Broadway toward Washington, where Route 57 becomes Washington Avenue through the commercial center. Beyond Port Colden and the Port Murray Road junction, the highway turns northeast beside the Musconetcong River, passing wooded areas and farmland toward Hackettstown.

moments.title: New Village
moments.text: A marker on Route 57 identifies a mile of road built in 1912 as New Jersey’s first concrete highway. Its cement came from Thomas Edison’s Portland Cement Company, founded in New Village in 1899. The company later supplied concrete for Yankee Stadium’s construction in 1922, then went bankrupt during the same decade. Remnants of the cement works can be found on nearby Edison Road. The highway also carries older history: its alignment west of Penwell was part of the Washington Turnpike, chartered in 1806. The marker places the 1912 concrete paving on that much older corridor of travel.

moments.title: Port Murray
moments.text: A surviving boat basin marks Port Murray’s place on the Morris Canal. The community was named for Colonel James Boyles Murray, the third president of the Morris Canal and Banking Company. From here to Saxton Falls, boats traveled eleven miles on one level. Elsewhere, the canal crossed hills with water-powered inclined planes: short railways carried boats uphill and down in open cars. Those devices connected stretches of water at different heights. Port Murray also had a station on the Morris and Essex Railroad, another transport link in the community. The Port Murray Historic District was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1996.

moments.title: Hackettstown
moments.text: At Florence Kuipers Memorial Park in Hackettstown, a mile of canal channel and towpath survives. A guard lock and towpath trail remain at Saxton Falls in Stephens State Park. Completion of the canal to Newark in 1831 had linked the coal trade with eastern cities before the later extension to Jersey City. The Morris Canal had carried coal to industrializing eastern cities, but railroads eroded its trade. It was formally abandoned in 1924 and largely dismantled over the following five years. These surviving stretches sit within a town in the Musconetcong River valley, where Route 57 reaches its eastern end.
